PAUT equipment: what a complete phased array kit includes

PAUT equipment is a system, not a single instrument. A working kit has six parts. The first is a phased array instrument sized by channel count, such as 16:64 or 32:128. Then come probes matched to thickness and material, and wedges for the refracted angle and pipe curvature. You also need an encoder and scanner for repeatable position, calibration blocks, and software that builds the scan plan and analyzes data. Choose each part around the welds you examine most.

Choosing a PAUT instrument: channels and capability

The two numbers on a phased array instrument describe its electronics. The first is how many pulser-receivers fire at once, which sets the largest active aperture. The second is how many probe elements the instrument can address through its multiplexer. A 16:64 unit fires 16 elements at a time anywhere along a 64-element probe. A 32:128 unit doubles both. "PR" after the numbers usually means each channel both pulses and receives.

Aperture matters because a larger active aperture focuses better at depth and puts more energy into thick or coarse-grained material. Most weld PAUT on plate and pipe of ordinary wall thickness runs well on 16 active elements. AWS D1.1 set a 16-channel instrument and a 16-element probe as minimums when it added its phased array annex in the 2020 edition. Thick sections, multi-probe setups and fast full matrix capture push you toward 32 or 64 active channels.

ConfigurationTypical fitWhere it runs out
16:64Weld PAUT on plate and pipe of ordinary wall, corrosion mapping with 64-element probes, structural work under AWS D1.1Heavy wall that needs larger focusing apertures; full matrix capture at production speed; several probes in one pass
16:128The same weld work, with 128-element probes for wider linear scans in corrosion mappingAperture is still 16, so focusing in thick sections is unchanged
32:128Thicker welds, two phased array probes plus a TOFD pair in one encoded pass, larger corrosion-mapping coverageMore setup and validation per job; more than routine shop welds need
64:128 and aboveHeavy-wall and nozzle work, full matrix capture and total focusing, qualification and research workRarely justified for routine field weld examination

Beyond channels, check these before choosing a model:

  • Multi-group capability. Can the instrument run two phased array groups and conventional channels for TOFD at once? Most in-lieu-of-RT setups need this.
  • Full matrix capture (FMC) and the total focusing method (TFM). These are useful for crack characterization and complex geometry. If you need them, check whether your code basis covers them before you pay for them.
  • Data rate and file size on long encoded scans, plus battery life and the operating temperature range for outdoor work on the Gulf Coast.
  • Software. Onboard scan-plan and weld-overlay tools, calibration wizards for every focal law, an offline analysis license, and export to your reporting system.

Portable units on the US market include the Evident OmniScan X3, the Eddyfi Gekko and Mantis, the Sonatest Veo3 and the Zetec Topaz. Atlantis does not sell equipment. Judge each one against your own weld mix, not a feature list.

Probes, wedges, encoders and scanners

Probes

Choose frequency by thickness and grain structure. Around 2.25 MHz suits thick or coarse-grained sections. Around 5 MHz is the usual choice for carbon steel welds. Use 7.5 to 10 MHz for thin wall and for resolving pitting in corrosion mapping. Element count and pitch set how far a linear scan reaches and how finely the beam steers. Elevation, the passive dimension, affects both coverage and how well the probe couples on curved pipe.

For austenitic stainless and dissimilar-metal welds, dual linear or dual matrix arrays help. They send and receive longitudinal waves on separate elements, which cuts noise from coarse grain and improves resolution near the surface. Matrix arrays also allow beam skewing for flaws that are not parallel to the weld.

Wedges

The wedge sets the range of refracted angles, typically a 40 to 70 degree shear-wave sweep for weld S-scans, or a 0 degree delay line for corrosion mapping. On pipe, the wedge must be contoured to the outside diameter once curvature would lift it off the surface. The procedure sets that threshold. Wedges wear, and a worn wedge changes the exit point and delay, so recheck wedge delay after heavy use. The wedge angle, velocity and height entered in the software must match the physical wedge, or every position you plot is wrong. Irrigated wedges help on long scans, and high-temperature wedges allow scans on hot surfaces within their rated limits.

Encoders

Encoded data is what makes PAUT auditable. Wheel encoders suit weld scanners. String encoders suit odd geometry. Calibrate the encoder over a known distance, and watch for wheel slip on wet or oily surfaces, which shows up as stretched or compressed data.

Scanners

Choose the scanner by access, not by catalog:

  • One-axis manual weld scanners with magnetic wheels for plate and large pipe
  • Chain or girth scanners for circumferential pipe welds
  • Low-profile scanners for small-bore pipe and tight clearance
  • Two-axis raster scanners or crawlers for corrosion mapping

Magnetic wheels do not hold on austenitic stainless, so plan for straps or vacuum mounts there.

Calibration blocks

You need Article 4 calibration blocks with side-drilled holes that match the material group, thickness range and curvature you examine. You also need a reference block for checking system performance, such as the ASTM E2491 assessment blocks. Code jobs that require procedure qualification also need demonstration blocks with known flaws. Order those early, because lead times are long.

Calibration and setup under ASME Section V Article 4

A correction first: phased array is not ASME Section V Article 11. Article 11 is acoustic emission of fiber-reinforced plastic vessels. PAUT sits inside Article 4, ultrasonic examination of welds, in its mandatory appendices:

  • Mandatory Appendix IV: phased array, single fixed angle, with manual raster scanning
  • Mandatory Appendix V: phased array E-scan and S-scan linear scanning with encoded data
  • Mandatory Appendix III: TOFD, often run in the same pass
  • Mandatory Appendix IX: procedure qualification, when flaw sizing or fracture-mechanics-based acceptance applies

Personnel add Article 1 Mandatory Appendix II. The full map is in our ASME Section V guide. A defensible encoded weld setup follows this sequence:

  1. Build the scan plan. Model the joint: thickness, bevel, weld cap and root, heat-affected zone, probe offset from the weld centerline, focal laws and angles. Then show that the beams cover the full examination volume. Save the plan with the data.
  2. Check the instrument. Run screen-height and amplitude-control linearity checks at the interval Article 4 and your procedure require.
  3. Check the probe. An element activity check finds dead or weak elements before they leave gaps in a sector.
  4. Calibrate wedge delay across all focal laws, so depth and position read correctly at every angle or index point.
  5. Set sensitivity across the whole sweep. Angle-corrected gain and a time-corrected gain curve on the side-drilled holes make one reflector read the same at every angle and depth.
  6. Calibrate the encoder over a known distance, and verify it again after any change.
  7. Prove coverage on the block. Confirm that the reflectors that matter show up where the scan plan says they will.
  8. Check the calibration at intervals and at the end. If a check fails, the data since the last good check is suspect and must be rescanned.
  9. Review data quality before you call anything. Look for coupling loss, encoder slip, saturation and missing lines. A poor-quality file is a rescan, not an interpretation.

ASTM E2491 in one paragraph

ASTM E2491 is the standard guide for evaluating the performance of phased array instruments and systems. The current edition is E2491-23. It describes checks for element activity, beam profile, steering capability, focusing and resolution using assessment blocks. It does not set acceptance criteria. It produces the data your procedure or client uses to set them. Run it when equipment is new, after repairs, and at the interval your written procedure sets. File the results with the instrument's calibration records. More detail is in our ASTM E2491 overview. ASTM E2700 is the companion practice for contact phased array examination of welds.

PAUT vs TOFD vs RT

Most US weld jobs choose between these three, or combine PAUT and TOFD to replace RT where the construction code allows ultrasonic examination in lieu of radiography.

CriterionPAUTTOFDRT
Best at detectingPlanar and volumetric flaws, including sidewall lack of fusion when the angles suit the bevelPlanar flaws in almost any orientation, through tip diffractionVolumetric flaws such as porosity and slag, and root profile
Height sizingGood, using tip diffraction or amplitude methods set by the procedureThe most accurate of the threeNo through-wall height
Weak spotsCoverage depends entirely on the scan plan; coarse-grain materialDead zones near the scanning surface and the backwallTight planar flaws not aligned with the beam; thick sections
RadiationNoneNoneExclusion zone; licensed crews under NRC or Agreement State rules
Effect on other workOther crafts keep workingOther crafts keep workingArea cleared during shots
RecordEncoded digital dataEncoded digital dataFilm or digital image
Section V basisArticle 4, Mandatory Appendices IV and VArticle 4, Mandatory Appendix IIIArticle 2
Typical US usePipe girth welds, vessel seams, structural welds, corrosion mappingThick welds, crack height for engineering assessmentThin wall, small bore, socket welds, and where the code or client requires RT

Buy PAUT equipment or hire a PAUT crew?

The instrument is the visible purchase. It is rarely the largest part of running PAUT in-house. Before you buy, count everything below:

  • Procedure development and Level III approval for each weld family you examine
  • Demonstration and qualification blocks with known flaws, where the code or client requires them
  • Technician training, supplemental technique qualification and practical exams under your written practice
  • Probes, wedges and scanners for each diameter and thickness range; wedges are consumables
  • Annual calibration, ASTM E2491 performance checks and repairs
  • Analysis software licenses, data storage and a reporting workflow
  • Utilization: kit that sits in a cage between turnarounds still costs money
Buy whenHire when
You have steady weekly PAUT volume on repeat weld typesDemand comes in turnaround or project peaks
You have, or can retain, a UT Level III to write and qualify proceduresEach job has new geometry, thickness or code basis
Your technicians already hold PAUT qualification and experienceYou need qualified people faster than you can train them
Your clients accept your in-house data without third-party reviewYour client or the code wants independent examination

Many fabricators split the difference. They buy one 16:64 kit for in-process checks and hire a crew for production PAUT, in-lieu-of-RT work and anything that needs procedure qualification. Atlantis performs PAUT with ASNT-certified technicians under ASNT Level III oversight. Field teams work from Houston across Texas, Louisiana and California. Pricing is quote on request, and we return a quote within 24 hours.

PAUT qualification: what US clients check

  • SNT-TC-1A or CP-189. PAUT is a technique within the UT method. Your written practice must define phased-array-specific training, experience and a practical exam on top of UT Level II. A UT Level II certificate alone does not cover phased array.
  • ASME Section V Article 1 Mandatory Appendix II. On Code work that invokes it, PAUT and TOFD personnel need supplemental training, experience and examinations in the technique, documented separately.
  • AWS D1.1 Annex H. Structural PAUT under the 2020 and later editions calls for written procedures, advanced training and qualification, and calibration specific to PAUT.
  • Owner performance demonstrations. Many refinery and pipeline owners require API's phased array examiner certification (QUPA) or crack-sizing certification (QUSE-PA). These are hands-on blind tests on flawed welds, valid for three years. Atlantis does not train for API certifications.
  • Acquisition vs analysis. Clients increasingly ask who interpreted the data and how that person is qualified, not just who held the probe.

Atlantis trains to ASNT SNT-TC-1A only, at Level I, II and III, live online or onsite at your facility, and has trained 1,000+ technicians. The phased array training course builds the technique hours and practical work your written practice requires. Our published US training fees list the costs.

Request a training plan for UT Level II technicians moving into phased array.

Common PAUT equipment and setup mistakes

  • Buying for the brochure. A 64-channel instrument for welds that never exceed ordinary wall thickness, with no budget left for procedures or blocks.
  • No scan plan on file. The S-scan looks thorough, but nothing proves the root and heat-affected zone were covered.
  • Calibrating one angle. Sensitivity set at 45 degrees, with the rest of the sweep left uncorrected.
  • Wedge parameters not updated after a wedge change, so every position is offset.
  • Treating encoded data as automatically valid. Encoder slip and coupling loss go unreviewed until an auditor finds them.
  • Raw files not kept. Without the data, a PAUT report is just an opinion. Store files with the asset. See storing and sharing PAUT scan data.

Not sure whether your next job needs PAUT, TOFD or RT? Request an inspection quote with the weld map and code, and we will recommend the method before pricing it. Service detail is on our phased array UT page.

Frequently asked questions

What is a PAUT machine, and how is it different from a conventional flaw detector?

A PAUT machine, or phased array instrument, fires many probe elements with timed delays to steer and focus the beam electronically. It records encoded images such as S-scans and C-scans. A conventional flaw detector drives one element at a fixed angle and shows a single A-scan trace. Most phased array instruments also run conventional UT and TOFD channels.

What is the best phased array ultrasonic testing equipment?

The best kit is the one that matches your weld mix, thickness range and code basis, with software your technicians and clients can work with. For ordinary-wall weld work, a 16:64 instrument with good scan-plan software is often enough. Thick sections, multi-probe setups and FMC justify 32 channels or more.

What does 16:64 or 32:128 mean on a PAUT instrument?

The first number is the active aperture: how many elements fire together. The second is how many elements the instrument can address on the probe. 16:64 means 16 elements fire at a time across a probe of up to 64 elements.

How do I select a phased array probe?

Start with frequency for thickness and grain, element count and pitch for coverage and steering, and elevation for coupling on curvature. Then choose a wedge for the angle range and pipe diameter. Austenitic and dissimilar welds usually need dual linear or dual matrix arrays.

What are the ASME requirements for phased array?

Under ASME Section V, phased array falls under Article 4 Mandatory Appendix IV for manual raster scanning and Appendix V for encoded E-scan and S-scan, with Appendix IX when procedure qualification applies. Personnel need Article 1 Mandatory Appendix II supplemental qualification. Acceptance criteria come from the construction code.

What goes into a PAUT procedure?

A PAUT procedure covers scope and code basis, materials and thickness range, instrument, probes and wedges, focal laws and scan plan, calibration and sensitivity method, encoder and scanner, scanning technique, data quality checks, recording and evaluation levels, personnel qualification and reporting. Variables the code marks essential must match what was demonstrated.

Do I need a scanner for PAUT?

You need one for encoded examination. Most code and in-lieu-of-RT work requires encoded data, and that means a scanner or at least an encoder. Manual raster PAUT without encoding exists under Appendix IV, but it leaves a weaker record.

What is matrix array UT (MAUT)?

Matrix array probes have elements in two directions, so the beam can be steered and skewed off the probe axis. They help with flaws not parallel to the weld, nozzle geometry, and dual matrix setups for austenitic material.

How do I get PAUT certification in the US?

You hold UT Level II under your employer's written practice, complete phased-array-specific training and logged experience, then pass the employer's PAUT exams, including a practical. Code work may add ASME Appendix II records, and some owners add API performance demonstrations.
